system_prompt:
You are a careful engineer. Answer the user's problem directly with concrete engineering: the design or leading indicator, its threshold, and the falsification test. Respect every stated constraint verbatim. English only. Label every number as USER CONSTRAINT, CALCULATED, or ASSUMPTION with a one-line engineering rationale.

FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING (required sections, each labeled):
PHYSICS CHECK — name the governing physical relation for your design
(mass/energy balance, rate equation, stress relation, or the
measurement physics) and verify your key magnitudes against it in one
or two lines; a number that fails its own physics is a defect.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — list the concrete means: components, materials,
instruments, and the procedure by which the change is built,
procured, or operated. Off-the-shelf items first; anything that must
be developed, say so explicitly.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — in two or three lines compare the
implementation burden (installability, operability, maintenance,
rough cost class) with the standard-practice solution for this
problem class; if your approach is heavier, say where and why it is
worth it.
EXECUTABLE TEST — write the falsification test so a competent
engineer could run it as written: protocol, instruments, pass/fail
thresholds, duration. A test that cannot be run is not a test.
a1_answer:
PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is Poiseuille's law for flow through a catheter (Q = Δπr⁴/8ηL), where pressure drop is proportional to flow rate and inversely proportional to catheter radius to the fourth power. A 20% delivery deficit creates a specific pressure signature detectable before occlusion, and fibrin deposition gradually reduces effective radius, increasing pressure at constant flow. USER CONSTRAINT: 20% delivery deficit threshold is clinically significant for glucose impact.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Add a dual-pressure sensor system: one at the pump outlet (existing) and one 5 cm from the cannula tip (new). Use a 0.5 mm diameter, 90 cm long silicone catheter with embedded micro-pressure transducers (off-the-shell, 0-300 mmHg range, ±1 mmHg accuracy). Signal processing compares pressure differentials to detect occlusions. Develop custom firmware to analyze pressure gradients and identify occlusion signatures before absolute pressure thresholds are reached. USER CONSTRAINT: Must maintain existing form factor, requiring miniaturized sensors.

STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — Current systems use single-point pressure detection with fixed thresholds, leading to missed partial occlusions. This dual-sensor approach adds minimal complexity (one additional sensor and firmware update) but significantly improves detection capability. Installation remains identical for patients, maintenance is unchanged, and cost increases by <15% for additional sensor. Worth it for preventing dangerous hyperglycemic episodes. ASSUMPTION: Current occlusion detection is single-point pressure-based.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Test 10 infusion sets with 5 each of complete occlusions (clamped at tip), partial occlusions (20% flow restriction via calibrated constriction), and slow leaks (0.5 mm hole at 30 cm mark). Instruments: Test rig with flow meter, pressure sensors, and glucose simulation system. Pass/fail: Complete occlusion must be detected within 15 minutes, partial occlusion within 2 hours, and no false alarms in 14 days of simulated wear (continuous 2 U/hr delivery with movement). Duration: 14 days continuous operation with daily movement simulation. CALCULATED: 20% flow restriction creates detectable pressure gradient change.
